source.title: Pew Research Center: How the Global Religious Landscape Changed From 2010 to 2020 (June 2025)

religions.label: Aboriginal Dreaming
religions.name: Aboriginal Australian religion
religions.story: No founder. The Dreaming grew with the first peoples of Australia over more than 50,000 years. It is handed down through song, dance, art and ceremony, each tied to a particular stretch of country.
religions.beliefs: Ancestral beings shaped the land in the Dreaming and remain present in it. Law, kinship and ceremony come from them, and songlines map the country.
religions.texts: None (oral tradition, song, dance and art)
religions.followers: Tens of thousands practise traditional forms
religions.origin: Australia; people have lived there at least 50,000 years
religions.founders: no founder; ancestral beings (e.g. the Rainbow Serpent, Baiame, Bunjil, the Wandjina); Elders as holders of Law
religions.branches: — (hundreds of distinct local traditions; Torres Strait Islanders have their own)
milestones: British First Fleet arrives, treating the land as unowned
Removal of children begins, the Stolen Generations era
Uluru handed back to its Anangu traditional owners
Mabo decision rejects terra nullius
National Apology to the Stolen Generations
sources: Wikipedia: Australian Aboriginal religion and mythology
religions.followersSource: Australian census 2021: 7,887 people named Aboriginal traditional religion; many more combine it with Christianity

religions.label: African traditional
religions.name: African traditional religions
religions.story: No founder. Hundreds of separate traditions grew with Africa's peoples (Yoruba, Akan, Igbo, Zulu and many more). Elders, diviners and healers pass them down by word of mouth.
religions.beliefs: Usually a distant creator god, with lesser gods and spirits closer to people. Ancestors stay part of the community; ritual keeps the world in balance.
religions.texts: None (oral; the Yoruba Ifá verses are a large oral corpus)
religions.followers: Tens of millions (often blended with Christianity or Islam)
religions.origin: Sub-Saharan Africa, prehistoric
religions.founders: No founder; carried by priests, diviners, spirit mediums, healers and sacred rulers
religions.branches: Hundreds of ethnic traditions, such as Yoruba, Akan, Igbo, Fon, Kongo, Dogon and Zulu
milestones: Ile-Ife bronze heads begin, linked to Yoruba kingship
Afonso I of Kongo makes Catholicism the court religion
Nongqawuse and the Xhosa cattle-killing
John Mbiti's African Religions and Philosophy
Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove becomes a World Heritage Site

religions.label: Native American
religions.name: Native American religions
religions.story: No founder. Each of hundreds of Native nations developed its own ceremonies and stories over thousands of years, rooted in its own land.
religions.beliefs: The world is alive with spirit. Right relationship with land, animals and ancestors; ceremonies such as the sweat lodge, Sun Dance and vision quest.
religions.origin: North America, prehistoric
religions.founders: No founder; prophets such as Handsome Lake (Seneca), Wovoka (Paiute) and Black Elk (Lakota)
religions.branches: Nation-specific traditions (Lakota, Hopi, Navajo, Haudenosaunee and hundreds more) plus pan-tribal movements such as the Native American Church
milestones: Earliest proposed date for the Haudenosaunee Great Law of Peace
Handsome Lake's visions found the Longhouse religion
Wounded Knee Massacre after Ghost Dance fears
Native American Church incorporated in Oklahoma
American Indian Religious Freedom Act passed
sources: Wikipedia: American Indian Religious Freedom Act

religions.label: Korean shamanism
religions.name: Korean shamanism (Muism)
religions.story: No founder. Shamanic rites go back to Korea's earliest kingdoms. Shamans, called mudang and mostly women, inherit the role or are called to it through a spirit illness.
religions.beliefs: Gods and spirits shape daily life. Shamans perform gut rituals to heal, bring luck and settle the restless dead.
religions.followers: Unmeasured; widely consulted in South Korea
religions.origin: Korean peninsula, prehistoric
religions.founders: No founder; the mythic founder-king Dangun, Princess Bari (in myth, ancestress of shamans), modern mudang such as Kim Keum-hwa (1931–2019)
religions.branches: No formal branches; regional styles of spirit-possessed and hereditary shamans
milestones: Dangun myth places the founding of Gojoseon in this year
Joseon's Neo-Confucian state ranks mudang in the lowest class
Donghak movement emerges from late Joseon popular religion
Saemaul Undong campaigns against shamanic shrines and gut
Jeju wind-goddess rite listed as UNESCO heritage

religions.label: Shinto
religions.name: Shinto
religions.story: No founder. Worship of kami at sacred rocks, trees and mountains goes back to prehistoric Japan. The imperial court wrote its myths down in the Kojiki (712) and Nihon Shoki (720), and the name Shinto came into use to set it apart from Buddhism.
religions.beliefs: Kami (spirits or gods) live in nature, places and ancestors. Purity and purification; shrine rituals and festivals; little formal doctrine.
religions.texts: Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (myth-histories, not scripture)
religions.followers: Most Japanese take part in rites; few identify only as Shinto
religions.origin: Japan; prehistoric roots, first written myths 712–720 CE
religions.founders: No founder; the imperial house (in myth descended from the sun goddess Amaterasu), Yoshida Kanetomo, Motoori Norinaga, Hirata Atsutane
religions.branches: Shrine Shinto, Imperial Household Shinto, Sect Shinto, folk Shinto; State Shinto existed 1868–1945
eras: Prehistory and the Yamato state (to 710 CE)
Nara and Heian: the great blending (710–1185)
Meiji to 1945: separation and State Shinto
milestones: Kojiki ties the imperial house to Amaterasu
Yoshida Kanetomo, founder of Yoshida Shinto, is born
Motoori Norinaga, Kokugaku leader, is born
Separation orders divide kami and buddhas; State Shinto era begins
Shinto Directive ends state support for Shinto

religions.label: Mesopotamia
religions.name: Mesopotamian religion
religions.endLabel: c. 79 CE, the last datable cuneiform tablet
religions.story: Grew in the first cities of Sumer, where each city had its patron god and temple. Cuneiform writing (c. 3200 BCE) recorded its myths. It faded under Persian and Greek rule.
religions.beliefs: Humans were made to serve the gods (An, Enlil, Enki, Inanna or Ishtar, Marduk). Temple cities and ziggurats, omens, and a gloomy underworld for everyone.
religions.texts: Enuma Elish, Epic of Gilgamesh, Atrahasis
religions.origin: Sumer, Akkad, Babylon and Assyria (modern Iraq), c. 3500 BCE
religions.founders: no founder; Enheduanna (priestess-poet), Hammurabi, Ashurbanipal, Nebuchadnezzar II
religions.branches: — (Sumerian, Babylonian and Assyrian phases)
eras: Old Babylonian and Kassite periods (c. 1900–1155 BCE)
milestones: Cuneiform writing appears, first for temple accounts
Sargon of Akkad unites the region
Cyrus of Persia takes Babylon
Last firmly datable cuneiform tablet, from Uruk
George Smith reads a Babylonian flood story

religions.label: Ancient Egypt
religions.name: Ancient Egyptian religion
religions.endLabel: c. 537 CE, when the temple at Philae closed
religions.story: Took shape from older local cults as the first pharaohs unified Egypt (c. 3100 BCE). It lasted more than 3,000 years until Christianity replaced it.
religions.beliefs: The pharaoh upholds ma'at, the cosmic order. Gods such as Ra, Osiris, Isis and Horus; in the afterlife the heart is weighed against the feather of ma'at.
religions.texts: Pyramid Texts, Coffin Texts, Book of the Dead
religions.origin: Nile valley, c. 3100 BCE (older prehistoric roots)
religions.founders: no founder; Imhotep (later deified), Akhenaten, the priesthoods of Ra and Amun
religions.branches: local theologies (Heliopolis, Hermopolis, Memphis, Thebes); Atenism
eras: Early Dynastic and Old Kingdom (c. 3100–2181 BCE)
Late, Ptolemaic and Roman periods (664 BCE – 4th c. CE)
milestones: Egypt unified; local gods form a shared pantheon
Akhenaten promotes the Aten almost alone
Last known hieroglyphic inscription carved at Philae
Champollion deciphers hieroglyphs
Kemetic Orthodoxy founded in the US

religions.label: Hinduism
religions.name: Hinduism
religions.story: No founder and no single starting point. It grew from the Vedic religion recorded in the Vedas (c. 1500–1200 BCE), possibly with Indus Valley roots, and absorbed many local traditions. The name Hinduism came much later.
religions.beliefs: Brahman and the true self (ātman); karma, rebirth and liberation (moksha); dharma. Many deities, often seen as faces of one divine.
religions.texts: Vedas, Upanishads, Bhagavad Gita, Ramayana, Mahabharata, Puranas
religions.origin: Indian subcontinent; roots in the Vedic period, c. 1500 BCE
religions.founders: no single founder; the Vedic seers (rishis), Adi Shankara, Ramanuja, Vivekananda, Gandhi
religions.branches: Vaishnavism, Shaivism, Shaktism, Smartism
eras: Indus Valley and the Vedic period (c. 2600–500 BCE)
Epics and the classical synthesis (c. 400 BCE – 550 CE)
Sultanates, Mughals and the northern saints (c. 1200–1750)
milestones: Rigveda composed orally, hymns to Indra and Agni
Oldest Upanishads turn to Brahman, atman and moksha
Gupta Empire: stone temples, Puranas and image worship spread
Adi Shankara systematizes Advaita Vedanta
Vivekananda presents Hinduism at Chicago Parliament of Religions

religions.label: Greek & Roman
religions.name: Greek and Roman religion
religions.endLabel: 391–392 CE, when Christian emperors banned sacrifice
religions.story: Grew from Minoan and Mycenaean cults; Zeus already appears on Linear B tablets. Homer and Hesiod gave Greeks a shared mythology, and Rome adopted many Greek gods.
religions.beliefs: The Olympian gods were honoured with sacrifice and civic festivals. Correct practice mattered more than belief; oracles and mystery cults.
religions.texts: No scripture; Homer and Hesiod as shared myth
religions.origin: Greece and Rome, c. 1500 BCE (Mycenaean Greece)
religions.founders: no founder; Homer and Hesiod (myths), Augustus (Roman revival), Julian (last pagan emperor)
religions.branches: civic cult, mystery cults, Roman state religion, imperial cult, philosophical religion
eras: Hellenistic world and Roman Republic (c. 509–31 BCE)
milestones: Homer and Hesiod give the gods their familiar stories
Socrates executed, partly on a charge of impiety
Augustus becomes pontifex maximus and restores temples
Theodosius I bans sacrifice and temple worship
Greece legally recognizes Hellenic religion

religions.label: Aztec & Maya
religions.name: Mesoamerican religion (Aztec and Maya)
religions.endLabel: 1521, the Spanish conquest of the Aztecs (the last Maya kingdom fell in 1697)
religions.story: Began with the Olmec (c. 1500 BCE) and passed to the Maya, Zapotec and Aztecs, who shared gods, calendars and ball-game rituals.
religions.beliefs: Gods of sun, rain, maize and the feathered serpent. Cyclical time and sacred calendars; blood offerings, including human sacrifice, repaid the gods.
religions.followers: Historical; survives blended into folk Catholicism
religions.origin: Mexico and Central America, c. 1500 BCE (Olmec)
religions.founders: No founder; gods such as Quetzalcoatl (Maya Kukulkan), Tlaloc (Maya Chaak) and Huitzilopochtli
religions.branches: Olmec, Zapotec, Teotihuacan, Maya, Mixtec and Aztec (Mexica)
milestones: Olmec build ceremonial centres at San Lorenzo and La Venta
Teotihuacan rises and builds the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon
Mexica found Tenochtitlan
Cortes and allies take Tenochtitlan
Guatemala's peace accords recognise Maya spirituality

religions.label: Chinese folk religion
religions.name: Chinese folk religion
religions.date: Prehistoric roots; first records c. 1250 BCE (Shang oracle bones)
religions.story: No founder. Ancestor worship and many local gods go back to prehistoric China. Oracle bones from the Shang dynasty (c. 1250 BCE) are its first written records.
religions.beliefs: Honour the ancestors and many gods (Mazu, the Kitchen God, the City God). Feng shui, divination and temple festivals; it blends freely with Taoism and Buddhism.
religions.origin: China; prehistoric roots, with written records from the Shang dynasty c. 1250 BCE
religions.founders: No founder; widely worshipped figures include the Jade Emperor, Guan Yu (Guandi), Mazu, Guanyin, the Earth God (Tudigong) and City Gods
religions.branches: No formal branches; local temple cults, lineage ancestor cults, spirit-medium cults and organized salvationist sects such as Yiguandao
milestones: Shang oracle bones put questions to ancestors and the high god Di
Mass worship of the Queen Mother of the West across north China
Song court elevates popular gods such as the Jade Emperor
Nationalist standards aim to abolish most cults and shrines
Mazu belief and customs listed as UNESCO intangible heritage

religions.label: Judaism
religions.name: Judaism
religions.date: c. 1200 BCE (Israelite religion); rabbinic Judaism after 70 CE
religions.rangeLabel: Monotheism took shape gradually, c. 1200–500 BCE
religions.story: Grew out of the religion of ancient Israel and Judah. Tradition traces it to Abraham's covenant and to Moses at Sinai. Historians see monotheism forming gradually, especially during the Babylonian exile (6th c. BCE). After the Temple fell in 70 CE, rabbinic Judaism took over.
religions.beliefs: One God made a covenant with Israel. Living by the Torah's commandments matters more than creed; hope for a messianic age.
religions.origin: Ancient Israel and Judah (Levant); Israelite religion c. 1200–500 BCE, rabbinic Judaism after 70 CE
religions.founders: in tradition Abraham and Moses; later Ezra, Yohanan ben Zakkai, Judah ha-Nasi, Rashi, Maimonides
religions.branches: Rabbinic Judaism (Orthodox, Conservative/Masorti, Reform, Reconstructionist) and the small Karaite community
eras: Exile and the Second Temple (587 BCE – 70 CE)
milestones: Merneptah Stele gives earliest outside mention of Israel
Babylon destroys the First Temple and deports Judah's elite
Rome destroys the Second Temple; rabbinic Judaism takes shape
Jews expelled from Spain
State of Israel declared on 14 May
religions.followersSource: Jewish Agency for Israel, estimate for Rosh Hashanah 2024

religions.label: Zoroastrianism
religions.name: Zoroastrianism
religions.rangeLabel: Zarathustra's date is debated: c. 1500–500 BCE
religions.story: Founded by the prophet Zarathustra (Zoroaster) in ancient Iran or Central Asia. He reformed the old Indo-Iranian religion, which Vedic India also grew from. It became the faith of the Persian empires.
religions.beliefs: The wise lord Ahura Mazda against the destructive spirit Angra Mainyu. Good thoughts, good words, good deeds; a final judgment and renewal of the world.
religions.origin: Ancient Iran / Central Asia, c. 1500–500 BCE (Zarathustra's date debated)
religions.founders: Zarathustra (Zoroaster); Sasanian high priests such as Kartir
religions.branches: Parsi and Irani communities; Shahenshahi, Qadimi and Fasli calendar groups
eras: Zarathustra and the Avestan age (c. 1500–550 BCE)
Seleucid and Parthian eras (330 BCE–224 CE)
Islamic conquest and minority life (633–19th c.)
milestones: Zarathustra's date is debated, placed as early as c. 1500 BCE
Cyrus the Great founds the Achaemenid Empire
Ardashir I makes Zoroastrianism the Sasanian state religion
Arab victory at Nahavand; the last king dies in 651
Iranshah sacred fire begins burning at Udvada
religions.followersSource: India census 2011 counted 57,264 Parsis; the worldwide figure is an estimate

religions.label: Polynesian
religions.name: Polynesian religion
religions.date: c. 1000 BCE onward, with the settlement of the Pacific
religions.story: Carried by voyagers settling the Pacific from about 1000 BCE; each island group adapted the shared gods and stories. Missionaries replaced it in the 1800s (Hawai‘i abolished its kapu system in 1819), and it has been revived since the 1970s.
religions.beliefs: Gods such as Tangaroa, Tāne, Tū and Rongo; the demigod Māui. Mana (spiritual power) and tapu or kapu (sacred restriction) order life.
religions.followers: Mostly replaced by Christianity; modern revivals
religions.origin: Polynesia; voyagers spread it from Tonga and Samoa (c. 1000 BCE) to Aotearoa New Zealand (c. 1300 CE)
religions.founders: no founder; priests (tohunga, kahuna) and chiefs; later Ka‘ahumanu, Pōmare II, Māori prophets
religions.branches: regional traditions (Hawaiian, Māori, Tahitian, Samoan, Tongan, Rapa Nui); Māori prophetic churches
eras: Settlement of the west (c. 1000 BCE – c. 900 CE)
Missions and the fall of the old order (1797–1840s)
milestones: Lapita voyagers reach Tonga and Samoa
Captain Cook reaches Hawai‘i
Hawaiian kapu system ended by Ka‘ahumanu and Keōpūolani
Tohunga Suppression Act outlaws traditional healers
Hōkūle‘a sails to Tahiti, sparking Hawaiian Renaissance

religions.label: Celtic
religions.name: Celtic religion
religions.date: c. 800 BCE (Hallstatt and La Tène cultures)
religions.endLabel: c. 6th century CE, as Christianity spread
religions.story: The religion of Europe's Iron Age Celtic peoples. Rome suppressed the druids, and Christianity replaced it by about the 6th century. The Celts wrote almost nothing down themselves.
religions.beliefs: Many local gods (Lugh, Brigid, the Dagda, Cernunnos). Sacred groves, springs and lakes; druids as priests, judges and teachers.
religions.texts: None (known from Roman writers and medieval Irish and Welsh tales)
religions.origin: Iron Age Gaul, Britain and Ireland, c. 800 BCE
religions.founders: no founder; the druids (priestly class); later Christian recorders in Ireland and Wales
religions.branches: — (Gaulish, British and Irish variants; Gallo-Roman fusion)
milestones: Iron Age Celtic cultures spread across Europe
Caesar conquers Gaul and describes the druids
Irish monks record myths in the Book of Leinster
Iolo Morganwg founds the Gorsedd of Bards
Order of Bards, Ovates and Druids founded

religions.label: Atheism & humanism
religions.name: Atheism, agnosticism and humanism
religions.date: Ideas from c. 600 BCE; organized humanism 19th–20th c.
religions.story: No founder. Doubt about the gods appears from about 600 BCE in ancient India (the Cārvāka school) and Greece (later Epicurus). It grew into modern atheism and secular humanism through the Enlightenment and the 19th and 20th centuries.
religions.beliefs: Atheism: no belief in gods. Agnosticism: whether gods exist can't be known. Secular humanism: ethics based on reason, science and human welfare.
religions.texts: No scripture; e.g. the Humanist Manifestos (1933, 1973, 2003)
religions.origin: Worldwide (ancient India and Greece; Enlightenment Europe); ancient ideas, organized humanism 19th–20th c.
religions.founders: no founder; key thinkers include the Carvaka school, Epicurus, Lucretius, Hume, d'Holbach, Darwin, Huxley and Russell
religions.branches: atheism, agnosticism, secular humanism, religious humanism, plus adjacent positions such as deism and pantheism
eras: Ancient India and China (c. 600 BCE–1000 CE)
Ancient Greece and Rome (c. 600 BCE–400 CE)
milestones: Carvaka materialist school arises in India
Poggio Bracciolini rediscovers Lucretius
T. H. Huxley coins the word agnostic
Soviet League of the Militant Godless founded
International Humanist and Ethical Union founded
religions.followersSource: Pew Research Center, 2025 report (2020 data): 24.2% of the world has no religious affiliation

religions.label: Jainism
religions.name: Jainism
religions.story: Taught in its present form by Mahavira (c. 6th–5th c. BCE), whom Jains see as the 24th and last Tirthankara of an eternal faith. It came out of the same movement of wandering ascetics as Buddhism.
religions.beliefs: Every living being has an eternal soul, and karma binds it. Liberation comes through strict non-violence (ahimsa), non-attachment and self-discipline.
religions.origin: Northeast India (today's Bihar), c. 6th–5th c. BCE
religions.founders: Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara; Parshvanatha, the 23rd; Kundakunda; Hemachandra
religions.branches: Digambara, Svetambara
eras: Mauryan patronage and the great split (c. 300 BCE – 500 CE)
milestones: Traditional birth date of Mahavira (historians place him later)
Chandragupta Maurya becomes a monk, in Digambara tradition
Svetambara canon written down at the Council of Valabhi
Statue of Bahubali carved at Shravanabelagola
Acharya Bhikshu founds the Terapanthi order

religions.label: Norse & Germanic
religions.name: Norse and Germanic paganism
religions.date: Iron Age, with Bronze Age roots
religions.story: Grew among the Germanic peoples from Bronze Age roots; best known from Viking-age Scandinavia. Kings converted to Christianity around 1000 (Iceland in 1000, Sweden by about 1100). Christians wrote the myths down in the 1200s.
religions.beliefs: Odin, Thor, Freyja and Freyr; the world tree Yggdrasil and nine worlds. Fate, honour and courage; Ragnarök, the end and rebirth of the world.
religions.texts: None originally; the Eddas were written down in the 1200s
religions.origin: Northern Europe and Scandinavia, Iron Age (Bronze Age roots debated)
religions.founders: no founder; later recorders Snorri Sturluson and Saxo Grammaticus
religions.branches: — (continental Germanic, Anglo-Saxon and Norse variants)
eras: Bronze Age and Roman Iron Age (c. 1700 BCE – 400 CE)
Migration period and continental conversion (c. 400–800 CE)
Romanticism, misuse and revival (19th c. – today)
milestones: Tacitus's Germania describes Germanic worship
Iceland's assembly accepts Christianity
Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda preserves the myths
Wagner's Ring cycle popularizes Norse myth
Ásatrúarfélagið founded in Iceland

religions.label: Confucianism
religions.name: Confucianism
religions.story: Started with Confucius (551–479 BCE), a teacher who wanted to restore the virtues and rites of the early Zhou dynasty. His students collected his sayings in the Analects, and the Han dynasty made it state orthodoxy.
religions.beliefs: A good society rests on good people: humaneness (ren), ritual propriety (li), filial piety and learning. Rulers govern by moral example.
religions.texts: Analects; the Four Books and Five Classics
religions.followers: Few formal adherents; shapes East Asian culture
religions.origin: State of Lu (Shandong, China), c. 500 BCE
religions.founders: Confucius (Kong Qiu, 551–479 BCE), Mencius, Xunzi, Dong Zhongshu, Zhu Xi, Wang Yangming
religions.branches: Classical Confucianism; Han state Confucianism; Neo-Confucianism (School of Principle, School of Mind); modern New Confucianism
eras: Confucius and the Warring States (c. 551–221 BCE)
Qin and Han: becoming state orthodoxy (221 BCE–220 CE)
Rivals and the Three Teachings (220–960 CE)
milestones: Confucius born in the state of Lu
Civil service examinations begin under the Sui
Zhu Xi's commentaries become the examination standard
Imperial examinations abolished
Red Guards damage Confucius sites at Qufu

religions.label: Buddhism
religions.name: Buddhism
religions.story: Founded by Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, who taught in northeast India after his enlightenment (c. 5th c. BCE). He came out of the movement of wandering ascetics who questioned Vedic ritual.
religions.beliefs: The Four Noble Truths: suffering comes from craving and can end (nirvana) through the Eightfold Path. No permanent self; karma and rebirth.
religions.texts: Pali Canon (Tipitaka), Mahayana sutras, Tibetan canon
religions.origin: Northeast India (Ganges plain), c. 5th c. BCE
religions.founders: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha; Ashoka; Nagarjuna; Padmasambhava; the Dalai Lamas; B. R. Ambedkar
religions.branches: Theravada, Mahayana, Vajrayana
eras: The Buddha and the early community (c. 5th–4th c. BCE)
Ashoka, Mahayana and the Silk Road (c. 268 BCE – 500 CE)
Vajrayana, Tibet and the Theravada world (c. 600–1500 CE)
milestones: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, lives and teaches in northeast India
Ashoka begins reign and promotes the Dharma through edicts
Buddhism reaches Korea
Atisha arrives in Tibet; four main schools take shape
Ambedkar and about 365,000 followers convert at Nagpur

religions.label: Taoism
religions.name: Taoism
religions.date: Philosophy c. 4th c. BCE; organized religion 142 CE
religions.rangeLabel: From the classical texts (c. 4th c. BCE) to the Celestial Masters (142 CE)
religions.story: No single founder. It grew from Chinese folk religion and from the philosophy of the Tao Te Ching (credited to Laozi) and the Zhuangzi. Zhang Daoling's Celestial Masters made it an organized religion in 142 CE.
religions.beliefs: Live in harmony with the Tao, the natural way of things. Effortless action (wu wei), simplicity, the balance of yin and yang; gods, rites and longevity practices.
religions.texts: Tao Te Ching, Zhuangzi, Daozang (the Taoist canon)
religions.origin: China; philosophy c. 4th c. BCE, organized religion from 142 CE
religions.founders: Laozi (traditional author of the Daodejing; his historicity is debated), Zhuangzi, Zhang Daoling, Ge Hong, Tao Hongjing, Wang Chongyang
religions.branches: Zhengyi (Celestial Masters) and Quanzhen (Complete Perfection); historically Shangqing and Lingbao
eras: Han dynasty and the first organized movements (206 BCE–220 CE)
New revelations and the Three Teachings (220–907 CE)
Song to Ming: new schools and the Canon (960–1644)
milestones: Daodejing takes shape; Guodian slips hold oldest passages
Laozi said to appear to Zhang Daoling, founding Celestial Masters
Wang Chongyang, founder of Quanzhen, dies
Ming prints the Zhengtong Daozang, the standard Canon
State-supervised Chinese Taoist Association founded

religions.label: Samaritanism
religions.name: Samaritanism
religions.rangeLabel: The split with Judaism is dated c. 5th–2nd c. BCE (debated)
religions.story: Samaritans and Jews both descend from the religion of ancient Israel. They split over where God should be worshipped: Mount Gerizim or Jerusalem. The split happened gradually.
religions.beliefs: Israelite faith centred on Mount Gerizim rather than Jerusalem. Only the five books of Moses are scripture; a priesthood descended from Aaron.
religions.origin: Samaria (Mount Gerizim); split from Judean religion c. 5th–2nd c. BCE (debated)
religions.founders: no founder; tradition looks to Moses and Joshua; later leaders include the high priest Baba Rabba and the poet-theologian Marqe (both 4th c. CE)
religions.branches: — (ancient sects such as the Dositheans died out)
eras: The Gerizim temple (c. 5th c. BCE – c. 110 BCE)
Roman and Byzantine eras (63 BCE – 636 CE)
milestones: Sacred precinct on Mount Gerizim exists by the 5th century BCE
John Hyrcanus destroys the Gerizim temple
Julianus ben Sabar's revolt against Byzantine rule begins
Only about 146 Samaritans remain, nearly all in Nablus
Community numbers about 900 in Holon and on Gerizim

religions.label: Tengrism
religions.name: Tengrism
religions.date: First recorded among the Xiongnu, c. 3rd c. BCE; revived in the 1990s
religions.story: No founder. Worship of Tengri, the Eternal Blue Sky, belonged to the peoples of the Eurasian steppe and is first recorded among the Xiongnu. It faded as Turks and Mongols turned to Islam and Buddhism, and revived after 1991.
religions.beliefs: Tengri, the Eternal Blue Sky, rules the world, with an Earth goddess. Spirits of nature and ancestors; shamans mediate between worlds.
religions.origin: Eurasian steppe (Mongolia, southern Siberia, Central Asia); ancient
religions.founders: no founder; Göktürk khagans, Chinggis Khan; modern revivalists
religions.branches: no single church; Mongolian and Siberian shamanism, Sakha Aiyy faith, Burkhanism, "political" Tengrism
eras: Steppe origins and the Xiongnu (c. 3rd c. BCE – 4th c. CE)
milestones: Xiongnu rulers' title read as an early form of Tengri
Bumin founds the First Turkic Khaganate
Temüjin proclaimed Chinggis Khan, claiming Eternal Heaven's mandate
Altan Khan titles Sonam Gyatso Dalai Lama; Mongols turn Buddhist
Tengir Ordo founded in Kyrgyzstan

religions.label: Christianity
religions.name: Christianity
religions.story: Began with Jesus of Nazareth, a Jewish teacher crucified in Jerusalem c. 30–33 CE. His followers proclaimed that he had risen from the dead, and Paul carried the message to non-Jews. It gradually separated from Judaism, became legal in the Roman Empire in 313 and its official religion in 380.
religions.beliefs: One God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Jesus is the Son of God, whose death and resurrection save humanity from sin; love of God and neighbour.
religions.origin: Roman Judea (Galilee and Jerusalem), c. 30 CE
religions.founders: Jesus of Nazareth; the apostles Peter and Paul; later Augustine, Aquinas, Luther, Calvin
religions.branches: Catholic; Protestant (including evangelical and Pentecostal); Eastern Orthodox; Oriental Orthodox; Church of the East
eras: Imperial church and the great councils (313–c. 600)
East and West in the Middle Ages (c. 600–1500)
The modern era and the global South (1900–today)
milestones: Jesus is crucified under Pilate; followers proclaim the Resurrection
Edict of Milan grants toleration to Christians
Great Schism between Rome and Constantinople
Luther's 95 Theses begin the Reformation
Azusa Street revival launches Pentecostalism

religions.label: Mandaeism
religions.name: Mandaeism
religions.rangeLabel: Origins are debated: c. 1st–3rd c. CE
religions.story: Its origins are debated. Mandaeans trace their faith to Adam and revere John the Baptist. Scholars place its beginnings among baptizing groups in the Jordan valley or southern Mesopotamia.
religions.beliefs: A God of Light far above the material world; the soul returns to the World of Light. John the Baptist is the great teacher; repeated baptism in flowing water.
religions.origin: Jordan valley and southern Mesopotamia, c. 1st–3rd c. CE (debated)
religions.founders: no founder; John the Baptist (Yahya Yuhana) is the most revered teacher
religions.branches: — (priests and laity; the most learned are called Nasoraeans)
milestones: Tradition says John the Baptist's disciples leave Jerusalem
Cholera in Shushtar kills almost all Mandaean priests
Persecution after the US-led invasion of Iraq begins
Iraq reserves a parliament seat for Mandaeans

religions.label: Manichaeism
religions.name: Manichaeism
religions.endLabel: c. 1600s, the last traces in southern China
religions.story: Founded by the prophet Mani (216–c. 277) in Sasanian Persia, who said he completed the work of Zoroaster, the Buddha and Jesus. It spread from the Roman Empire to China, then was persecuted almost everywhere.
religions.beliefs: A cosmic war of Light against Darkness. Light trapped in matter is freed by strict, ascetic living.
religions.origin: Sasanian Persia (Mesopotamia), c. 240 CE
religions.founders: Mani (216–c. 277 CE); the Uyghur ruler Bögü Qaghan
religions.branches: a western church led from Babylonia; the eastern Dēnāwar branch; Chinese Mingjiao
eras: Persecution in the Roman world (3rd–6th c.)
The Silk Road and the Uyghurs (6th–11th c.)
milestones: Mani is born near Ctesiphon
Bögü Qaghan makes Manichaeism the Uyghur state religion
Ming dynasty bans the Religion of Light
Manichaeism fades out; no continuous community survives
Turfan finds begin recovery of lost Manichaean texts

religions.label: Islam
religions.name: Islam
religions.rangeLabel: From the first revelation (610) to Muhammad's death (632)
religions.story: Began in 610 CE when Muhammad, a merchant of Mecca, reported revelations from God through the angel Gabriel. Persecuted in Mecca, he moved to Medina in 622 (the Hijra, year 1 of the Islamic calendar), where the first Muslim community formed.
religions.beliefs: Submission to the one God, Allah. Muhammad is the final prophet; the Five Pillars are faith, prayer, charity, fasting and pilgrimage.
religions.origin: Mecca and Medina, Arabia; 610 CE (first revelation), 622 CE (Hijra)
religions.founders: the Prophet Muhammad (c. 570–632), whom Muslims see as the last of many prophets rather than a founder; the first caliphs Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali; the Shia Imams
religions.branches: Sunni (~85–90%), Shia (~10–15%), Ibadi (small); Sufism runs across them
eras: The Rashidun caliphs and the first civil war (632–661)
milestones: Muslims date Muhammad's first revelation to 610
The Hijra to Medina marks year 1 of the Islamic calendar
Mongols sack Baghdad
Safavids make Twelver Shiism Iran's state religion
Turkey abolishes the caliphate

religions.label: Druze
religions.name: Druze faith
religions.story: Began in 1017 in Fatimid Cairo, when preachers led by Hamza ibn Ali proclaimed a new message about the caliph al-Hakim. It grew out of Ismaili Islam into a separate faith and stopped accepting converts in 1043.
religions.beliefs: The absolute unity of God. Souls are reborn at once into new human bodies; inner teachings are kept for initiates.
religions.origin: Fatimid Egypt, then the Levant, 1017 CE
religions.founders: Fatimid caliph al-Ḥākim bi-Amr Allāh (r. 996–1021), the preacher Ḥamza ibn ‘Alī, and Bahā’ al-Dīn al-Muqtanā
religions.branches: — (the community divides into initiated ‘uqqāl and uninitiated juhhāl)
milestones: The Divine Call opens publicly under Fatimid caliph al-Ḥākim
Al-Muqtanā closes the Call to new members
Mount Lebanon civil war between Druze and Maronites
Sultan Pasha al-Aṭrash leads the Great Syrian Revolt
Deadly clashes in Suwayda, Syria

religions.label: Yazidism
religions.name: Yazidism
religions.date: 12th c. CE (Sheikh Adi), with older roots
religions.story: Grew from the Sufi order of Sheikh Adi ibn Musafir (d. 1162), who settled at Lalish in northern Iraq. In the Kurdish mountains it mixed with older local beliefs and became a religion of its own.
religions.beliefs: One God entrusted the world to seven angels led by Tawûsî Melek, the Peacock Angel. Rebirth of souls; members are born, not converted.
religions.origin: Northern Iraq (Lalish), 12th c. CE (Sheikh Adi), with older roots
religions.founders: Sheikh Adi ibn Musafir (d. 1162); Tawûsî Melek, the Peacock Angel; the Mir and the Baba Sheikh
milestones: Sheikh Adi dies; his tomb at Lalish becomes the holiest shrine
Sheikh Hasan is executed by the ruler of Mosul
Suicide bombings kill 796 people in Qahtaniya and Jazira
ISIS overruns Sinjar and begins the Yazidi genocide
UN Commission of Inquiry finds genocide

religions.label: Yarsanism
religions.name: Yarsanism
religions.story: Organized by Sultan Sahak in the 14th century in the Kurdish region of western Iran. It came out of the Shia and Sufi world of the time and older Iranian beliefs.
religions.beliefs: God appears in human form in successive eras, above all as Sultan Sahak. Rebirth of souls; sacred music on the tanbur; communal gatherings (jam).
religions.origin: Western Iran (Kurdish region), 14th c. CE (Sultan Sahak)
religions.founders: Sultan Sahak (late 14th c.); the Haft Tan, led by Pir Binyamin; Ostad Elahi (20th c.)
religions.branches: eleven hereditary spiritual houses (khandans); "separate religion" and Shia-leaning interpretations
eras: Sultan Sahak and the founding (late 14th–15th c.)
Reform and the modern state (20th c.)
milestones: Sultan Sahak, seen by adherents as a manifestation of God, teaches
Kalam-e Saranjam, the teachings of Sultan Sahak, gathered
Ostad Elahi's circle teaches Yarsanism as a universal path
Iraqi Kurdistan recognizes the Kaka'i community

religions.label: Inca
religions.name: Inca religion
religions.date: The Inca state, c. 1400 CE, on older Andean roots
religions.story: The Inca state (c. 1400–1532) built an empire-wide cult of the sun god Inti on top of much older Andean beliefs. The Spanish conquest ended the state religion; worship of Pachamama and sacred places survived.
religions.beliefs: The sun god Inti, ancestor of the Inca rulers; the creator Viracocha; Earth Mother Pachamama; sacred places and objects (huacas).
religions.origin: Andes (Peru), Inca state c. 1400–1532 CE, on older Andean roots
religions.founders: No founder; tradition credits the ruler Pachacuti (r. c. 1438–1471) with reshaping state religion
milestones: Caral builds early monumental platforms
Pachacuti reshapes state religion and rebuilds the Coricancha
Pizarro seizes Atahualpa at Cajamarca
Taki Onqoy movement preaches against the Spanish
Inti Raymi re-enactment begins at Sacsayhuaman

religions.label: Sikhism
religions.name: Sikhism
religions.story: Founded by Guru Nanak (1469–1539) in Punjab, who after a spiritual experience around 1499 taught that "there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim". Nine more Gurus followed; Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa in 1699.
religions.beliefs: One formless God (Ik Onkar). Equality of all regardless of caste or gender; remembering God, honest work, sharing and selfless service.
religions.origin: Punjab (now split between India and Pakistan), c. 1500 CE
religions.founders: Guru Nanak (1469–1539) and nine successor Gurus, ending with Guru Gobind Singh
religions.branches: mainstream Khalsa tradition; Namdhari, Nirankari, Udasi, Nihang
eras: Guru Nanak and the early Gurus (1469–1606)
milestones: Guru Nanak born at Talwandi
Guru Arjan compiles the Adi Granth
Guru Gobind Singh creates the Khalsa at Vaisakhi
Britain annexes Punjab after two Anglo-Sikh Wars
Operation Blue Star and the anti-Sikh riots

religions.label: African diaspora
religions.name: African diaspora religions (Vodou, Santería, Candomblé)
religions.rangeLabel: Formed during the Atlantic slave trade, 16th–19th c.
religions.story: Enslaved Africans brought to the Americas kept their Yoruba, Fon and Kongo gods alive, often hidden behind Catholic saints. This gave rise to Vodou in Haiti, Santería in Cuba, and Candomblé and later Umbanda in Brazil.
religions.beliefs: Spirits (orishas, lwa) are served with drumming, dance, offerings and trance possession, often paired with Catholic saints.
religions.origin: Caribbean and Brazil, from Yoruba, Fon and Kongo roots, 16th–19th c. CE (Umbanda in the early 20th c.)
religions.founders: No founder; created by enslaved Africans and their descendants; noted priestesses include Marie Laveau and Mãe Menininha do Gantois
religions.branches: Haitian Vodou, Cuban Santería (Lucumí) and Palo, Brazilian Candomblé and Umbanda, Trinidad Orisha, Louisiana Voodoo, Surinamese Winti
milestones: Bois Caïman ceremony said to begin the Haitian Revolution
Date adherents give for the birth of Umbanda in Rio
Haiti's anti-superstition campaign destroys temples
US Supreme Court protects Santería animal sacrifice
Haiti recognizes Vodou as a religion
religions.followersSource: Brazil census 2022: 1.8 million followers of Umbanda and Candomblé

religions.label: Latter Day Saints
religions.name: Latter Day Saint movement
religions.story: Founded by Joseph Smith in New York in 1830, after he reported visions and published the Book of Mormon. It came out of the revivals of the Second Great Awakening. After Smith's murder in 1844, Brigham Young led most members to Utah.
religions.beliefs: Christ's original church restored through Joseph Smith. Father, Son and Holy Ghost are separate beings; living prophets; families sealed for eternity in temples.
religions.texts: Bible, Book of Mormon, Doctrine and Covenants, Pearl of Great Price
religions.origin: western New York, USA; church organized 6 April 1830
religions.founders: Joseph Smith (1805–1844); Brigham Young; Joseph Smith III; Russell M. Nelson (president 2018–2025); Dallin H. Oaks (president since 2025)
religions.branches: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints; Community of Christ; Mormon fundamentalists
milestones: Date Joseph Smith later gave for his First Vision
Church organized on 6 April; Book of Mormon published
Wilford Woodruff's Manifesto ends new plural marriages
Kimball announces end of the priesthood ban for Black men
Nelson asks that the full church name be used
sources: Wikipedia: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
religions.followersSource: Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints statistical report for 2025, plus other Latter Day Saint churches

religions.label: Bahá’í Faith
religions.name: Bahá’í Faith
religions.rangeLabel: From the Báb's announcement (1844) to Bahá’u’lláh's declaration (1863)
religions.story: Grew out of the Bábí movement: in 1844 in Iran, the Báb announced that a new messenger was coming. In 1863 Bahá’u’lláh, one of his followers, declared in exile in Baghdad that he was that messenger.
religions.beliefs: One God sends messengers age by age. The unity of humanity and of religions; equality of women and men; harmony of science and religion.
religions.texts: Writings of the Báb, Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu'l-Bahá
religions.origin: Qajar Iran, 1844 (the Báb); 1863 (Bahá’u’lláh)
religions.founders: the Báb (1819–1850), Bahá’u’lláh (1817–1892), ‘Abdu’l-Bahá (1844–1921), Shoghi Effendi (1897–1957)
religions.branches: one main community led by the Universal House of Justice; a few tiny breakaway groups
eras: Persecution in Iran and global growth (1979–present)
milestones: The Báb declares his mission in Shiraz
The Báb is executed in Tabriz
Bahá’u’lláh declares his mission in the Garden of Riḍván
First Universal House of Justice is elected
Persecution of Bahá’ís in Iran intensifies after the revolution

religions.label: Spiritism
religions.name: Spiritism
religions.story: Set out by the French teacher Allan Kardec, whose The Spirits' Book (1857) organized messages said to come from spirits through mediums. It came out of the table-turning craze of the 1850s and took deepest root in Brazil.
religions.beliefs: God and immortal spirits that reincarnate to improve morally. Mediums can talk with spirits; charity and self-improvement.
religions.texts: The Spirits' Book and Kardec's other works
religions.origin: Paris, France, 1857 (publication of The Spirits' Book)
religions.founders: Allan Kardec (1804–1869); Léon Denis; Bezerra de Menezes; Chico Xavier (1910–2002); Divaldo Franco (1927–2025)
religions.branches: religious ("Christian") Spiritism; a smaller secular-philosophical current
eras: Decline in France, growth in the Americas (1869–1930)
Chico Xavier and the Brazilian flowering (1930–2002)
milestones: Fox sisters report spirit rappings in Hydesville
Kardec publishes The Spirits' Book
Chico Xavier begins publishing spirit-dictated books
International Spiritist Council founded
Brazil counts 1.8% of its population as Spiritist

religions.label: Cheondoism
religions.name: Cheondoism
religions.story: Founded as Donghak ("Eastern Learning") in 1860 by Choe Je-u after a religious experience, as a Korean answer to Western ideas and Catholicism. It was renamed Cheondogyo in 1905.
religions.beliefs: Humans are Heaven: the divine Hanulnim lives in every person, so all people are equal. Social reform.
religions.followers: Tens of thousands in South Korea; North Korea reports ~15,000
religions.origin: Joseon Korea (near Gyeongju), 1860
religions.founders: Choe Je-u (1824–1864), Choe Si-hyeong (1827–1898), Son Byong-hi (1861–1922)
religions.branches: Cheondogyo; small offshoots such as Sicheongyo
milestones: Choe Je-u reports a revelation from the Lord of Heaven
Choe Je-u executed in Daegu
Donghak Peasant Revolution begins at Gobu
Son Byong-hi renames Donghak as Cheondogyo
Cheondoists among signers of March 1st Movement declaration
religions.followersSource: North Korea’s 2002 report to the UN Human Rights Committee, as cited by the US State Department

religions.label: Jehovah's Witnesses
religions.name: Jehovah's Witnesses
religions.rangeLabel: Bible Students in the 1870s; named Jehovah's Witnesses in 1931
religions.story: Started in the 1870s with Charles Taze Russell's Bible Student group in Pennsylvania, out of Adventist expectation of Christ's return. The group took the name Jehovah's Witnesses in 1931 under Joseph Rutherford.
religions.beliefs: Jehovah is the one God and Jesus is his son, not God himself. God's Kingdom will soon replace human governments; door-to-door preaching; no blood transfusions.
religions.origin: Allegheny (now Pittsburgh), Pennsylvania, USA; 1870s, name adopted 1931
religions.founders: Charles Taze Russell (1852–1916); Joseph F. Rutherford (1869–1942); Nathan H. Knorr; the Governing Body (Warwick, New York)
religions.branches: one centrally run organization; small independent Bible Student groups share its roots
milestones: Russell launches Zion's Watch Tower
Bible Students adopt the name Jehovah’s Witnesses
Nazi Germany bans the Witnesses
Authority passes to the Governing Body
Russia's Supreme Court declares the organization extremist
sources: Wikipedia: Persecution of Jehovah's Witnesses in Nazi Germany
religions.followersSource: Jehovah’s Witnesses 2025 service year report (peak publishers)

religions.label: Caodaism
religions.name: Caodaism
religions.story: Founded in 1926 in southern Vietnam after séances in which, followers say, the Supreme Being spoke to the civil servant Ngô Văn Chiêu (from 1921) and others. It deliberately blends Buddhism, Taoism, Confucianism, Christianity and spiritism.
religions.beliefs: One Supreme Being, shown as the Divine Eye, unites the great religions. Its saints include Victor Hugo; vegetarianism, prayer and séances.
religions.texts: Collected spirit messages and the religion's constitution
religions.origin: Southern Vietnam (Saigon and Tây Ninh), 1926
religions.founders: Ngô Văn Chiêu (first disciple), Lê Văn Trung (first acting pope), Phạm Công Tắc (chief medium)
religions.branches: Tây Ninh Holy See (largest); about ten smaller recognized sects
milestones: Ngô Văn Chiêu said to receive messages from God on Phú Quốc
Religion declared to the French governor, then inaugurated at Tây Ninh
Ngô Đình Diệm breaks the armed sects
Communist government seizes property and bans séances
Vietnam recognizes the Tây Ninh Holy See

religions.label: Rastafari
religions.name: Rastafari
religions.story: Grew in 1930s Jamaica among poor Black Jamaicans after Haile Selassie was crowned emperor of Ethiopia in 1930, which many saw as fulfilling Marcus Garvey's call to look to Africa. Street preachers such as Leonard Howell spread it.
religions.beliefs: God (Jah) is revealed in Haile Selassie I. Africa (Zion) against an oppressive Babylon; natural ital living; dreadlocks; ganja as a sacrament for many.
religions.origin: Jamaica, 1930s
religions.founders: no single founder; early preachers Leonard Howell, Joseph Hibbert, Archibald Dunkley and Robert Hinds; inspired by Marcus Garvey; Emperor Haile Selassie I of Ethiopia revered as divine (a status he never claimed)
religions.branches: the "mansions" Nyabinghi, Bobo Ashanti and Twelve Tribes of Israel
milestones: Ras Tafari is crowned Emperor Haile Selassie I
Haile Selassie visits Jamaica to huge crowds
Bob Marley dies and becomes the movement's global icon
Jamaica allows Rastafari sacramental cannabis use
religions.followersSource: Jamaica census 2011 counted 29,026; the worldwide figure is an estimate

religions.label: Wicca & Paganism
religions.name: Wicca and modern Paganism
religions.story: Made public by Gerald Gardner in England in the early 1950s. He said it was a surviving witch religion, which historians doubt. It drew on folklore, ceremonial magic and romantic ideas about Europe's pagan past.
religions.beliefs: A Goddess and a God; eight seasonal festivals (the Wheel of the Year); ritual magic; the ethic "an it harm none, do what ye will".
religions.texts: None central; covens keep a Book of Shadows
religions.origin: England, 1950s (Wicca); wider Pagan revival, 20th c.
religions.founders: Gerald Gardner (1884–1964); Doreen Valiente (1922–1999); Alex and Maxine Sanders; Starhawk; Ross Nichols (Druidry); Sveinbjörn Beinteinsson (Heathenry)
religions.branches: Wicca (Gardnerian, Alexandrian, eclectic, Dianic, Reclaiming); Druidry; Heathenry; reconstructionist paths
eras: Roots in Romanticism and the occult (1700s–1930s)
Gardner and the birth of Wicca (1939–1964)
milestones: Iolo Morganwg holds the first Gorsedd of Bards in London
Margaret Murray publishes The Witch-Cult in Western Europe
Witchcraft Act repealed; Gardner goes public in 1954
Buckland brings Gardnerian Wicca to the USA
Starhawk publishes The Spiral Dance

religions.label: Scientology
religions.name: Scientology
religions.story: Founded by the science-fiction writer L. Ron Hubbard. He published Dianetics as a self-help therapy in 1950, then recast it as a religion; the first churches were incorporated in 1953–54.
religions.beliefs: Humans are immortal spiritual beings (thetans). Auditing removes past traumas to reach the state of Clear. Highly controversial.
religions.followers: Claims ~10 million; independent estimates in the tens of thousands
religions.origin: USA, 1953–54 (Dianetics 1950)
religions.founders: L. Ron Hubbard (1911–1986); David Miscavige (leader since the 1980s)
religions.branches: Church of Scientology; independent "Free Zone" Scientologists
eras: Snow White and Hubbard's last years (1973–1986)
milestones: Hubbard publishes Dianetics
Church of Scientology of California registered
Hubbard founds the Sea Organization
IRS grants tax exemption to the church
French court convicts church bodies of organised fraud
religions.followersSource: A 2008 US survey found about 25,000 adult adherents

religions.label: Unitarian Universalism
religions.name: Unitarian Universalism
religions.rangeLabel: Unitarian churches from 1568; the merger in 1961
religions.story: Formed in 1961 when the American Unitarian and Universalist churches merged. Both grew out of Protestant Christianity: Unitarians from 16th-century anti-Trinitarians, Universalists from the belief that all souls will be saved.
religions.beliefs: No required creed; members may be theist, atheist, Buddhist, Pagan or other. Shared values: dignity, justice, a free search for truth and care for the earth.
religions.origin: USA, 1961 merger; roots in 16th-c. CE European anti-Trinitarianism
religions.founders: Michael Servetus, Ferenc Dávid, Joseph Priestley, William Ellery Channing, Hosea Ballou
religions.branches: Unitarian and Universalist heritages; national bodies in the USA, Canada, Britain, Transylvania and India
milestones: Servetus attacks the Trinity; burned in Geneva in 1553
Edict of Torda grants preachers religious freedom in Transylvania
American Unitarian Association formed
Unitarian and Universalist bodies merge as the UUA
General Assembly approves new Article II
religions.followersSource: Unitarian Universalist Association, about 130,000 adult members in 2024

religions.label: Falun Gong
religions.name: Falun Gong
religions.story: Introduced by Li Hongzhi in China in 1992, during a boom in qigong (breathing and exercise practice). He added moral teachings drawn from Buddhism and Taoism. China banned it in 1999.
religions.beliefs: Truthfulness, compassion, forbearance. Meditation and slow exercises cultivate body and mind; banned and persecuted in China since 1999.
religions.origin: Changchun, northeast China, 1992
religions.founders: Li Hongzhi (born 1951 or 1952; the date is disputed), based in the USA since 1998
religions.branches: — (no formal branches; affiliated media and arts groups abroad)
milestones: Li Hongzhi first teaches Falun Gong in Changchun
Zhuan Falun published as the core text
About 10,000 practitioners gather at Zhongnanhai on 25 April
Government bans Falun Gong on 22 July
Kilgour-Matas report alleges organ harvesting, which China denies
religions.followersSource: Freedom House (2017) estimated 7–20 million practitioners in China
